title: August | 2026 | FRED Blog
gist: A FRED Blog post (Aug 3, 2026) contrasts non-seasonally adjusted construction employment in Minnesota vs Kentucky (May 2016–June 2026) and finds both states peak in August and trough in February, but Minnesota's seasonal swing as a share of seasonally adjusted employment is far wider than Kentucky's — the author attributes it to Southern crews being able to work through more of the winter. Note: the raw record title is the archive-page title 'August | 2026 | FRED Blog'; the actual body is this single construction-employment post.

insights.claim: Non-seasonally adjusted construction employment in both Minnesota and Kentucky follows the same annual shape — rising through August and declining until February — but the amplitude of that swing is far wider in Minnesota than in Kentucky.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Anyone reading state-level construction payrolls or building-materials demand off raw monthly prints must know the August peak / February trough calendar, and that the same headline delta means very different things in a Northern vs a Southern state.
insights.quote: increases through August and declines until February, but a much wider seasonal range in Minnesota than in Kentucky
insights.locator: To better tell the story behind the numbers

insights.claim: The FRED Blog attributes the wider seasonal swing in Northern-state construction employment to winter workability: crews in the South can keep working through more of the winter months than crews in the North, compressing the South's seasonal trough.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Gives a weather-workability mechanism for regional construction-labor and materials demand — a mild or harsh winter should move Northern-state activity far more than Southern-state activity, which matters for regionally exposed builders, aggregates and rental-equipment demand.
insights.quote: This difference could be related to the ability to work through more of the winter months in the South relative to the North.

insights.claim: Minnesota and Kentucky were deliberately chosen as a construction-seasonality contrast because they have markedly different winter and summer weather, making state climate — not state industry mix — the framing variable for the comparison.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A reusable screen: when comparing regional labor data in weather-exposed industries, sort states by climate first, because climate can dominate the raw seasonal signal.
insights.locator: We picked those two states to make our point

insights.claim: Because Minnesota has far more construction employees than Kentucky, comparing raw annual employment peaks and troughs between the two states in levels is misleading; the blog normalizes by plotting the seasonal change as a fraction of seasonally adjusted employment.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A transferable normalization for any cross-region labor or activity comparison: express the NSA-minus-SA gap as a share of the SA level so state size drops out and only seasonal intensity remains.
insights.quote: Given this size difference, comparing annual employment peaks and throughs between states isn’t easy or straightforward.
insights.locator: Note there are far more construction employees

insights.claim: The gap between a not-seasonally-adjusted series and its seasonally adjusted twin is itself a usable measurement of how weather-exposed an industry is in a given state, rather than just a data-cleaning artifact to be discarded.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Treat the SA/NSA spread as a free weather-sensitivity indicator you can compute for any state or industry pair in FRED, and use it to rank regional exposure to abnormal winters.
insights.locator: The dashed lines are the same employment figures

insights.claim: The exact BLS state construction-employment series needed to replicate this weather-sensitivity analysis are MNCONS and KYCONS (seasonally adjusted) and MNCONSN and KYCONSN (not seasonally adjusted), monthly, available in FRED from at least May 2016 through June 2026.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Concrete tickers to pull for a monitoring dashboard — and the same CONS/CONSN naming pattern extends to every other state, so the seasonal-amplitude screen can be run nationwide.
